title: Inorder Traversal
description:
Given a binary tree, return the inorder traversal of its nodes' values.
Inorder: Left → Root → Right
story: Inorder walks left-subtree first, then visits root, then right-subtree. For a BST, inorder gives sorted ascending order.
plain: Inorder means you first visit the entire left subtree recursively, then process the current node, then visit the entire right subtree. It's called 'inorder' because in a Binary Search Tree, this produces values in sorted order. You accumulate results in a list as you visit nodes.
tale: Imagine you're walking through an art gallery arranged as a tree. The rule is: always explore every room to your left before admiring the current painting, then every room to your right. So you walk all the way left until you hit a wall, admire the leftmost painting, backtrack one room, admire that painting, then explore the right side. When you're done, you've seen every painting in perfect left-to-right order, the way they were meant to be viewed.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Use recursion. The base case is when you hit null — just return. Otherwise, recurse left, add the current node's value to your result list, then recurse right. The recursion stack uses O(H) space where H is the height of the tree.
solutions.tale: You're a traveler with a notebook. At each tree node, you whisper 'go left first' to yourself. You walk all the way left until you can't anymore. Then you write down what you see. Then you whisper 'now go right' and repeat. The whispers are recursive calls. Your notebook fills itself in perfect inorder as you backtrack.
approach: If the node is null, return immediately (base case).
Recursively traverse the left subtree.
Add the current node's value to the result list.
Recursively traverse the right subtree.
Return the accumulated result list.
solutions.pseudocode:
inorder(node, result):
  if node == null: return
  inorder(node.left, result)
  result.add(node.val)
  inorder(node.right, result)
solutions.story: Left first, me next, then right. Recurse.

title: Preorder Traversal
description:
Given a binary tree, return the preorder traversal of its nodes' values.
Preorder: Root → Left → Right
story: Preorder visits the root first, then left subtree, then right. It's the order you'd write if you were copying the tree structure top-down.
plain: Preorder means you process the current node immediately, then recursively visit the entire left subtree, then the right subtree. The name 'preorder' means 'root comes before (pre) the children'. You accumulate values in a list as you visit each node.
tale: You're a scout mapping a cave system. At every junction, you immediately mark the current room on your map before exploring deeper. You always explore the left tunnel first, marking every room you find. When the left tunnel ends, you backtrack and explore the right tunnel, again marking each room as soon as you enter it. Your map fills in the exact order you discovered rooms — root first, then everything to the left, then everything to the right.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Use recursion. Base case: if node is null, return. Otherwise, add the current node's value to the result list first, then recurse left, then recurse right. The recursion stack depth is the height of the tree.
solutions.tale: You're a traveler who writes down every landmark the instant you see it. You see the root — you write it. You walk left and see another node — you write it immediately. You keep walking left, writing each node the moment you arrive. When you hit a dead end, you backtrack and explore right, again writing each node on first sight. Your notebook fills in discovery order.
approach: If the node is null, return immediately (base case).
Add the current node's value to the result list.
Recursively traverse the left subtree.
Recursively traverse the right subtree.
Return the accumulated result list.
solutions.pseudocode:
preorder(node, result):
  if node == null: return
  result.add(node.val)
  preorder(node.left, result)
  preorder(node.right, result)
solutions.story: Me first, then left, then right. Recurse.

title: Path Sum (Root to Leaf)
description:
Given a binary tree and a sum, determine if the tree has a root-to-leaf path such that adding up all the values along the path equals the given sum.

Return 1 if such path exists, else return 0.
story: Walk every root-to-leaf path accumulating sum. At each leaf, check if the running sum equals target. Return 1 if any path works.
plain: You want to find if there exists any path from root to leaf where the node values sum to a target. You use DFS to explore all paths. At each node, add its value to a running sum. When you reach a leaf (no children), check if the running sum equals the target. If any path works, return true. If all paths fail, return false.
tale: Imagine you're a hiker climbing a mountain network. At each junction, you add the elevation change to your total climb. Some trails end at a peak, others at a valley. You're looking for any trail that ends at a peak with a total climb of exactly 22 meters. You explore every trail recursively — at each junction you go left first, then right. When you hit a dead end (a leaf), you check your total. If it matches 22, you've found the path. If not, you backtrack and try another trail.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Use recursion with a running sum. Base case: if node is null, return false. If it's a leaf, return whether the running sum plus node value equals target. Otherwise, recurse left and right with updated sum. Use OR to short-circuit — if left path works, don't check right.
solutions.tale: You're an explorer with a sum counter. At each cave room, you add its treasure value to your counter. When you reach a dead end, you check if your counter matches the goal. If it does, you yell success and the echo carries back up all the recursive calls. If not, you backtrack and try another tunnel. The OR operator is your echo — once any path yells success, the whole recursion returns true.
approach: If the node is null, return false (no path here).
Add the current node's value to the running sum.
If it's a leaf node (no children), check if running sum equals target.
If not a leaf, recursively check left subtree OR right subtree.
Return true if either subtree has a valid path, else false.
solutions.pseudocode:
hasPathSum(node, target, sum):
  if node == null: return false
  sum += node.val
  if isLeaf(node): return sum == target
  return hasPathSum(left, target, sum) OR hasPathSum(right, target, sum)
solutions.story: Accumulate sum top-down. At leaf, check if sum matches target.

title: Equal Tree Partition
description:
Given a binary tree A. Check whether it is possible to partition the tree to two trees which have equal sum of values after removing exactly one edge on the original tree.

Return 1 if the tree can be partitioned into two trees of equal sum else return 0.
story: Compute every subtree sum. Store in map. If total sum is even and half-sum exists in map, return 1.
plain: To partition a tree into two equal-sum parts, you need to find a subtree whose sum is exactly half the total tree sum. Compute subtree sums bottom-up using post-order traversal. Store each subtree sum in a hash map. After computing the total sum, check if it's even. If yes, check if the map contains totalSum/2. If yes, cutting that subtree creates two equal parts.
tale: Imagine a kingdom where each village (node) has treasure. You're tasked with splitting the kingdom fairly by cutting one road. You walk through every village bottom-up, tallying treasure in each region. You write down every region's total in a ledger. At the end, you know the kingdom's total wealth. If it's an odd number, no fair split exists. If even, you check your ledger: does any region have exactly half the treasure? If yes, cut the road to that region — both sides now have equal wealth.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Use post-order traversal to compute subtree sums. At each node, sum = left + right + node.val. Store every subtree sum in a HashMap. After full traversal, check if totalSum is even. If yes, query the map for totalSum/2. Be careful: don't count the root's total as a valid cut (you can't remove the root). Use a count-based map or remove the root entry before checking.
solutions.tale: You're a tax collector visiting every village. At each leaf village, you note its treasure. As you backtrack, you sum up the children villages and add the current village's treasure. You write every regional total in your book. When you reach the capital (root), you know the kingdom's wealth. If it's odd, impossible. If even, you flip through your book looking for exactly half. If you find it, mark that village as the cut point.
approach: Define a post-order helper that returns subtree sum.
At each node, compute left sum, right sum, then total = left + right + node.val.
Store the total in a HashMap with node reference or sum count.
After traversal, check if totalSum is even.
If even, query map for totalSum / 2 (excluding root's entry).
Return 1 if found, 0 otherwise.
solutions.pseudocode:
postorder(node, map):
  if node == null: return 0
  left = postorder(node.left, map)
  right = postorder(node.right, map)
  sum = left + right + node.val
  map[sum] += 1
  return sum
solutions.story: Compute subtree sums, store in map. If totalSum even and halfSum in map → valid cut.

title: Postorder Traversal
description:
Given a binary tree, return the postorder traversal of its nodes' values.
Postorder: Left → Right → Root
story: Postorder visits children before parent. Used for deletion (delete children first, then parent) and bottom-up computations.
plain: Postorder means you visit the left subtree first, then the right subtree, then the current node. The name 'postorder' means the root comes after (post) the children. This is useful when you need to process children before their parent, like when deleting a tree or computing subtree properties.
tale: You're an archaeologist excavating a buried city. The rule is: you must fully explore and document every tunnel before you can document the chamber you're in. So you go left as far as you can, documenting the deepest rooms first. Then you backtrack and explore right, again documenting deepest first. Only after all tunnels are mapped do you write down the current room. Your map fills from leaves to root.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Use recursion. Base case: if node is null, return. Otherwise, recurse left, recurse right, then add the current node's value to the result list. The key is adding the node value LAST, after both children are fully processed.
solutions.tale: You're a cleanup crew. You can't remove a room until all rooms below it are cleared. So you go all the way down the left tunnel, clearing the deepest room. You backtrack and do the same for the right tunnel. Only when both tunnels below a room are clear do you remove that room. The recursion stack ensures you always clear children before parents.
approach: If the node is null, return immediately (base case).
Recursively traverse the left subtree.
Recursively traverse the right subtree.
Add the current node's value to the result list.
Return the accumulated result list.
solutions.pseudocode:
postorder(node, result):
  if node == null: return
  postorder(node.left, result)
  postorder(node.right, result)
  result.add(node.val)
solutions.story: Left first, then right, me last. Recurse.

title: Sum Binary Tree Check
description:
Given a binary tree, check whether it is a Sum-binary Tree or not.

Sum-binary Tree is a Binary Tree where the value of every node is equal to sum of the nodes present in its left subtree and right subtree.

An empty tree is Sum-binary Tree and sum of an empty tree can be considered as 0. A leaf node is also considered as SumTree.

Return 1 if it is sum-binary tree else return 0.
story: Post-order traversal returns subtree sum if valid, -1 if broken. Parent checks if leftSum + rightSum equals its value. One mismatch bubbles -1 up the entire chain.
plain: A Sum Tree means every node's value equals the sum of its left and right subtrees. You validate this bottom-up using post-order recursion. At each node, recursively get the left and right subtree sums. If either is -1 (invalid), bubble -1 up. If they sum to the node's value, return the total sum of the subtree (left + right + node). If they don't match, return -1. Leaves are always valid and return their own value.
tale: Imagine you're an auditor checking if every warehouse's inventory matches the sum of its two sub-warehouses. You start at the deepest sub-warehouses (leaves) — they're always correct because they have no children. As you climb up, you ask each warehouse: does your inventory equal the sum of your left and right sub-warehouses? If yes, you record the total inventory for that entire branch (left + right + current). If no, you mark the entire tree as broken and stop. One bad warehouse ruins the whole chain.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Use post-order recursion. Base case: null returns 0, leaf returns its value. For internal nodes, get left and right subtree sums. If either is -1 (invalid subtree), return -1. If leftSum + rightSum equals node value, return leftSum + rightSum + node value (total subtree sum). Otherwise return -1. The main function checks if the result is -1.
solutions.tale: You're a tree inspector with a rule: every parent must equal the sum of its children. You start at the leaves — they're always valid, so you write down their values. As you backtrack to each parent, you check: does parent = left child + right child? If yes, you write down the total for that entire branch (left + right + parent) and move up. If no, you write '-1' (broken) and that -1 propagates all the way to the top. One broken node breaks the whole tree.
approach: Base case: if node is null, return 0.
Base case: if node is a leaf, return node.val.
Recursively compute left subtree sum.
Recursively compute right subtree sum.
If either subtree returns -1, return -1 (invalid tree).
Check if node.val equals leftSum + rightSum.
If yes, return leftSum + rightSum + node.val (total subtree sum).
If no, return -1 (invalid tree).
Main function returns 1 if result ≠ -1, else 0.
solutions.pseudocode:
sumBinaryTreeOrNot(node):
  if node == null: return 0
  if node is leaf: return node.val
  leftSum = sumBinaryTreeOrNot(node.left)
  rightSum = sumBinaryTreeOrNot(node.right)
  if leftSum == -1 or rightSum == -1: return -1
  if leftSum + rightSum == node.val:
    return leftSum + rightSum + node.val
  else:
    return -1
solutions.story: Post-order: children first, parent checks sum, bubble up total or -1.

title: Level Order Traversal
description:
Given a binary tree, return the level order traversal of its nodes' values. (i.e., from left to right, level by level).

Return a 2D integer array denoting the level order traversal of the given binary tree.
story: BFS with a queue. Process all nodes at one level before moving to the next. Track level size to group nodes into separate lists.
plain: Level order means you visit nodes level by level, left to right. Use a queue and BFS (breadth-first search). Start by adding the root to the queue. For each level, count how many nodes are in the queue (that's the level size). Dequeue that many nodes, add them to the current level's list, and enqueue their children. Repeat until the queue is empty. The key is tracking the level size before processing it.
tale: You're photographing a family reunion where people stand in rows by generation. You take one photo per generation. You start with the grandparents (root), then their children (next level), then grandchildren. You use a waiting line (queue). For each photo, you count how many people are in line, photograph exactly that many, then ask their children to join the line. You never mix generations in a single photo because you count before you shoot.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Use a queue. Add root to queue. While queue is not empty, record the queue size (this is the current level size). Dequeue that many nodes, add their values to a temporary list, and enqueue their children. Add the temporary list to the result. Repeat. Space is O(W) where W is the maximum width of the tree (largest level size).
solutions.tale: You're a tour guide leading groups floor by floor through a museum. At each floor, you count how many people are with you. You show them that floor's exhibits, then send them to the next floor's entrance. Their children join the group at the next floor. You never mix floors because you count your group size before starting each tour.
approach: Create a result list (2D array) and a queue.
Add the root to the queue.
While queue is not empty:
Record the current queue size (levelSize).
Create an empty list for this level.
For i = 0 to levelSize-1: dequeue a node, add its value to the level list, enqueue its children.
Add the level list to the result.
Return the result.
solutions.story: Queue + level-size tracking. Process each level as a batch before moving to the next.

title: Build Tree from Inorder and Postorder
description:
Given the inorder and postorder traversal of a tree, construct the binary tree.

NOTE: You may assume that duplicates do not exist in the tree.
story: Postorder's last element is the root. Find it in inorder to split left/right subtrees. Recurse with updated ranges. Track indices carefully.
plain: Postorder's last element is always the root. Find that root in the inorder array — everything to its left is the left subtree, everything to its right is the right subtree. Recursively build left and right subtrees by adjusting start/end indices in both arrays. Use index arithmetic to map inorder ranges to postorder ranges. The number of elements in the left subtree determines where to split the postorder array.
tale: You're an archaeologist reconstructing a building from two lists: the order rooms were built (postorder) and the order they appear left-to-right (inorder). The last room built is always the central hall (root). You find the central hall in the layout list — everything left of it is the west wing, everything right is the east wing. You recursively rebuild each wing using the same logic: the last-built room in that wing's build list is that wing's center.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Use recursion with index ranges. Base case: if start > end, return null. Root is postorder's last element in the current range. Find root in inorder to get left subtree size. Compute new ranges for left and right subtrees using arithmetic. Left subtree uses postorder[post_s..r-1] and inorder[in_s..index-1]. Right subtree uses postorder[r..post_e-1] and inorder[index+1..in_e]. Build recursively.
solutions.tale: You're a puzzle solver with two clues. Clue 1 (postorder) tells you the last piece placed in each section. Clue 2 (inorder) tells you the left-to-right order of pieces. You pick the last piece from the build order — that's the center. You find it in the layout order and split: everything to its left is the left puzzle, everything to its right is the right puzzle. You count the left pieces to figure out how many build-order entries belong to the left puzzle. Recurse on each half.
approach: Base case: if start index > end index, return null.
Root value is the last element in the current postorder range.
Create a TreeNode with root value.
Find the root's index in the inorder array.
Count left subtree size: index - in_s.
Compute r (right boundary of left subtree in postorder): r = in_s + post_s + (left size - 1).
Recursively build left subtree: postorder[post_s..r-1], inorder[in_s..index-1].
Recursively build right subtree: postorder[r..post_e-1], inorder[index+1..in_e].
Return the root node.
solutions.pseudocode:
buildTree(post, in, post_s, post_e, in_s, in_e):
  if in_s > in_e: return null
  rootVal = post[post_e]
  root = new TreeNode(rootVal)
  index = find rootVal in in[in_s..in_e]
  leftSize = index - in_s
  r = post_s + leftSize - 1
  root.left = buildTree(post, in, post_s, r, in_s, index-1)
  root.right = buildTree(post, in, r+1, post_e-1, index+1, in_e)
  return root

title: Balanced Binary Tree Check
description:
Given a root of binary tree A, determine if it is height-balanced.

A height-balanced binary tree is defined as a binary tree in which the depth of the two subtrees of every node never differ by more than 1.

Return 0 / 1 ( 0 for false, 1 for true ) for this problem.
story: Post-order: compute left and right heights. If either child is unbalanced (-2), bubble -2 up. If height difference > 1, return -2. Else return max height + 1.
plain: A tree is balanced if at every node, the left and right subtree heights differ by at most 1. Use post-order recursion to compute heights bottom-up. At each node, get the left and right subtree heights. If either is -2 (unbalanced sentinel), return -2. If their absolute difference exceeds 1, return -2. Otherwise, return the max of the two heights plus 1. The main function checks if the result is -2.
tale: You're a structural engineer inspecting a tower made of blocks. The tower is safe if at every junction, the left and right branches differ in height by at most 1 block. You start at the bottom, measuring each branch's height. As you climb, you check each junction: if the left and right differ by more than 1, you mark the whole tower as unsafe (-2) and stop. If a subtower below was already unsafe, that mark bubbles up. Only if all junctions pass do you report the total height.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Use post-order recursion. Base case: null returns -1 (height of empty tree). For each node, recursively get left and right heights. If either is -2 (unbalanced), return -2. Check if |leftHeight - rightHeight| > 1. If yes, return -2 (unbalanced). Otherwise, return max(leftHeight, rightHeight) + 1. The main function returns 0 if result is -2, else 1.
solutions.tale: You're a tower inspector with a rule: no junction can have branches differing by more than 1 level. You start at the leaves — they're all height 0 (counting edges, or -1 if counting as empty below). As you backtrack to each parent, you ask: do my left and right children differ by more than 1? If yes, you stamp the whole tower 'UNSAFE' (-2) and that stamp propagates all the way up. If no, you write down the taller child's height plus 1. One unsafe junction ruins the whole tower.
approach: Base case: if node is null, return -1 (empty tree height).
Recursively compute left subtree height.
Recursively compute right subtree height.
If left height is -2, return -2 (left subtree unbalanced).
If right height is -2, return -2 (right subtree unbalanced).
If |leftHeight - rightHeight| > 1, return -2 (current node unbalanced).
Otherwise, return max(leftHeight, rightHeight) + 1.
Main function: return 1 if result ≠ -2, else 0.

isBalanced(node):
  if node == null: return -1
  leftHeight = isBalanced(node.left)
  rightHeight = isBalanced(node.right)
  if leftHeight == -2 or rightHeight == -2: return -2
  if |leftHeight - rightHeight| > 1: return -2
  return max(leftHeight, rightHeight) + 1

title: Left View of Binary Tree
description:
Given a binary tree of integers. Return an array of integers representing the left view of the Binary tree.

Left view of a Binary Tree is a set of nodes visible when the tree is visited from Left side.

NOTE: The value that comes first in the array which have lower level.
story: Level-order BFS. For each level, add the first node visited to the result. Track a flag per level to ensure only the leftmost is added.
plain: Left view means the leftmost visible node at each level. Use BFS with level tracking. Process nodes level by level. For each level, maintain a flag to record only the first node encountered (leftmost). As you dequeue nodes, if the flag shows you haven't added a leftmost node yet for this level, add the current node and set the flag. Continue processing the level, enqueuing children, but don't add more nodes to the result for this level.
tale: You're a photographer standing to the left of a tree. You take one photo per level, capturing only the leftmost node you can see. You use a queue to visit nodes level by level. At each level, you mark the first node you see as the 'leftmost' and snap a photo. Even if you see more nodes at that level as you move right, you don't take more photos — one per level is enough. You move down to the next level and repeat.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Use BFS with a queue. Add root to queue and result. While queue is not empty, record level size. For each node in the level, dequeue it. If it's the first node of this level (tracked by a boolean flag), add it to the result. Enqueue its children (left first, then right). Reset the flag for the next level. Space is O(W) for the queue.
solutions.tale: You're a scout mapping visible landmarks from the left side of a mountain range. At each elevation (level), you note the first peak you see. You use a line of explorers (queue) to systematically visit peaks left-to-right, elevation by elevation. For each elevation, you mark the first peak in your notebook, then send scouts to check lower elevations. You never mark a second peak at the same elevation — the first one blocks the view.
approach: Create a result list and a queue.
Add root to queue and to result (root is always visible).
While queue is not empty:
Record level size.
Set a flag isLeftMostAdded = false.
For each node in the level:
Dequeue the node.
If flag is false and node has a left child, add left child to result and set flag = true.
If flag is false and node has a right child, add right child to result and set flag = true.
Enqueue left and right children.
Return result.
solutions.pseudocode:
leftView(root):
  result = [root.val]
  queue.add(root)
  while queue not empty:
    levelSize = queue.size()
    leftAdded = false
    for i = 0 to levelSize-1:
      node = queue.dequeue()
      if not leftAdded and node.left:
        result.add(node.left.val)
        leftAdded = true
      if not leftAdded and node.right:
        result.add(node.right.val)
        leftAdded = true
      enqueue children
  return result

title: Build Tree from Preorder and Inorder
description:
Given preorder and inorder traversal of a tree, construct the binary tree.

NOTE: You may assume that duplicates do not exist in the tree.
story: Preorder's first element is the root. Find it in inorder to split left/right subtrees. Recurse with updated ranges. Similar to postorder version but root comes first.
plain: Preorder's first element is always the root. Find that root in the inorder array — everything to its left is the left subtree, everything to its right is the right subtree. Recursively build left and right subtrees by adjusting start/end indices in both arrays. The number of elements in the left subtree (from inorder) tells you where to split the preorder array. Left subtree uses preorder[pre_s+1..r] and inorder[in_s..index-1]. Right subtree uses preorder[r+1..pre_e] and inorder[index+1..in_e].
tale: You're a detective reconstructing a crime scene from two witness accounts. Witness 1 (preorder) describes the order the rooms were entered (root first). Witness 2 (inorder) describes the left-to-right layout of rooms. The first room entered is always the main hall (root). You find the main hall in the layout list — everything left is the west wing, everything right is the east wing. You count the west wing rooms to figure out how many 'entered-first' entries belong to that wing. Recurse on each wing.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Use recursion with index ranges. Base case: if start > end, return null. Root is preorder's first element in the current range. Find root in inorder to get left subtree size. Compute new ranges: left subtree uses preorder[pre_s+1..r] and inorder[in_s..index-1]. Right subtree uses preorder[r+1..pre_e] and inorder[index+1..in_e]. Where r = pre_s + (index - in_s). Build recursively.
solutions.tale: You're assembling a family tree from two logs. Log 1 (preorder) lists people in the order they arrived at the reunion (parent before kids). Log 2 (inorder) lists their seating arrangement left-to-right. The first arrival is always the family head (root). You find them in the seating chart and split: left seats are left branch, right seats are right branch. You count the left seats to know how many arrivals belong to the left branch. Recurse on each branch with the correct slice of the arrival log.
approach: Base case: if start index > end index, return null.
Root value is the first element in the current preorder range.
Create a TreeNode with root value.
Find the root's index in the inorder array.
Count left subtree size: index - in_s.
Compute r (right boundary of left subtree in preorder): r = pre_s + leftSize.
Recursively build left subtree: preorder[pre_s+1..r], inorder[in_s..index-1].
Recursively build right subtree: preorder[r+1..pre_e], inorder[index+1..in_e].
Return the root node.
solutions.pseudocode:
buildTree(pre, in, pre_s, pre_e, in_s, in_e):
  if pre_s > pre_e: return null
  rootVal = pre[pre_s]
  root = new TreeNode(rootVal)
  index = find rootVal in in[in_s..in_e]
  leftSize = index - in_s
  r = pre_s + leftSize
  root.left = buildTree(pre, in, pre_s+1, r, in_s, index-1)
  root.right = buildTree(pre, in, r+1, pre_e, index+1, in_e)
  return root
solutions.story: Preorder's first = root. Find it in inorder to split. Recurse with range arithmetic.

title: Serialize Binary Tree (Level Order)
description:
Given the root node of a Binary Tree, serialize it into an integer array denoting the Level Order Traversal of the given Binary Tree.

NOTE:
• In the array, the NULL/None child is denoted by -1.
• For more clarification check the Example Input.
story: BFS but write everything down, including the gaps.
plain: Serialize means convert the tree structure into a flat array that can be stored or transmitted. Use level-order traversal with a queue. For each node you pop, write its value to the output array, then enqueue its left and right children. If a child is null, enqueue null anyway so you can write -1 to mark the gap. Stop when the queue is empty.
tale: Imagine you are a scribe chronicling a royal family tree. You stand at the palace gates and call out the king's name first. Then you write down his two children — left prince, right prince — even if one throne is empty (you write 'vacant' for empty thrones). Then you move to the next generation, calling each person's name and recording their children. By the end, your scroll is a single line of names and gaps, but anyone reading it can rebuild the entire tree exactly as it stood, generation by generation.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Use a queue for BFS. Start with the root. While the queue is not empty, pop a node. If it's null, write -1 and continue. Otherwise, write its value, then enqueue its left and right children (even if they're null). The result array captures the tree structure level by level with -1 marking absent nodes.
solutions.tale: The scribe stands with a queue of parchment slips, each bearing a noble's name. He picks the first slip (the king), writes the name, then adds slips for the king's children to the back of the queue — even blank slips for missing heirs. He repeats: pick, write, add children. When the queue is empty, his scroll is complete, a perfect replica in ink.
approach: Initialize an empty result list and a queue containing the root node.
While the queue is not empty, dequeue the front node.
If the node is null, append -1 to the result and continue.
Otherwise, append the node's value to the result.
Enqueue the node's left child (even if null).
Enqueue the node's right child (even if null).
Return the result list.
solutions.pseudocode:
ans = []
queue = [root]
while queue not empty:
  cur = queue.pop()
  if cur == null:
    ans.append(-1)
    continue
  ans.append(cur.val)
  queue.enqueue(cur.left)
  queue.enqueue(cur.right)
return ans

title: Deserialize Binary Tree (from Level Order)
description:
You are given an integer array A denoting the Level Order Traversal of the Binary Tree.

You have to Deserialize the given Traversal in the Binary Tree and return the root of the Binary Tree.

NOTE:
• In the array, the NULL/None child is denoted by -1.
• For more clarification check the Example Input.
story: Read the array in pairs. The first number is a parent, the next two are its children.
plain: Deserialize is the reverse of serialize: rebuild the tree from the flat array. Use a queue and an index pointer. Create the root from A[0]. Enqueue it. While the queue is not empty and index < array length, pop a node. Read the next two values from the array: left child (index i) and right child (index i+1). If a value is -1, that child is null. Otherwise, create the child node, attach it, and enqueue it. Advance the index by 2.
tale: You are a gardener with a scroll listing tree nodes level by level, gaps marked 'vacant'. You read the first name and plant a seed — that's the root. Then you look at the scroll: the next two names are its children. You plant them (or leave soil empty for vacants) and tie them to the root. Now you pick the leftmost planted sapling and repeat: read its two children from the scroll, plant, tie. Move to the next sapling in line. By the time you reach the end of the scroll, the tree stands exactly as it was when the scribe recorded it.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Start with the first element as root. Use a queue. An index pointer walks the array. For each node in the queue, the next two elements in the array are its left and right children. Create nodes for non -1 values, attach them, and enqueue them. Skip nulls. The queue ensures level-order construction.
solutions.tale: The gardener starts with the king's name and a queue of planted saplings awaiting their heirs. She picks the first sapling, reads the scroll for its two children, plants them (or marks empty spots), adds them to the queue. She moves to the next sapling. The scroll unrolls steadily; the queue shrinks as she plants the last leaves. The tree is reborn.
approach: If the array is empty or A[0] is -1, return null.
Create root from A[0] and enqueue it. Set index i = 1.
While queue is not empty and i < array length, pop the current node.
Read A[i]: if not -1, create left child, attach it, enqueue it.
Increment i.
Read A[i]: if not -1, create right child, attach it, enqueue it.
Increment i.
Return the root.
solutions.pseudocode:
if A is empty or A[0] == -1: return null
root = new TreeNode(A[0])
queue = [root]
i = 1
while queue not empty and i < len(A):
  cur = queue.pop()
  leftVal = A[i++]
  if leftVal != -1:
    cur.left = new TreeNode(leftVal)
    queue.enqueue(cur.left)
  rightVal = A[i++]
  if rightVal != -1:
    cur.right = new TreeNode(rightVal)
    queue.enqueue(cur.right)
return root

title: Right View of Binary Tree
description:
Given a binary tree of integers denoted by root A. Return an array of integers representing the right view of the Binary tree.

Right view of a Binary Tree is a set of nodes visible when the tree is visited from Right side.
story: Level-order traversal, but only remember the last node of each level.
plain: Do a level-order BFS with a queue. For each level, process all nodes in that level (track the level size). The last node you process in each level is the rightmost visible node from the right side — add its value to the result. Repeat until the tree is fully traversed.
tale: Imagine standing at the right edge of a forest where the trees are planted in neat rows, each row slightly behind the last. You can only see the rightmost tree in each row because the others are hidden behind it. You walk forward row by row, noting down the rightmost tree each time. When you reach the back of the forest, your list is complete: the right-side silhouette of the entire grove.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Use BFS with a queue. For each level, count how many nodes are in that level. Process all of them in a loop. The last node processed in each level is the rightmost — add its value to the result list. Enqueue children as usual. Continue until the queue is empty.
solutions.tale: The observer carries a rope with knots, one knot per row of trees. She stands at the first row, counts the trees, walks through them left to right, and when she reaches the last tree, she writes its name on her parchment. She moves to the next row, repeats. Her parchment collects only the rightmost names, row by row, until the forest ends.
approach: If the root is null, return an empty list.
Initialize a result list and a queue with the root.
While the queue is not empty, note the current level size.
Loop through all nodes at this level: dequeue, enqueue children.
The last node dequeued in this loop is the rightmost → add it to result.
Repeat for all levels.
Return the result list.

title: Valid Binary Search Tree
description:
You are given a binary tree represented by root A. You need to check if it is a Binary Search Tree or not.

Assume a BST is defined as follows:
1) The left subtree of a node contains only nodes with keys less than the node's key.
2) The right subtree of a node contains only nodes with keys greater than the node's key.
3) Both the left and right subtrees must also be binary search trees.
story: Every node must satisfy: left subtree < node < right subtree. Pass min/max bounds down.
plain: A BST is valid if every node's value falls within a valid range determined by its ancestors. For the root, the range is (-∞, +∞). When you go left, the max becomes the current node's value. When you go right, the min becomes the current node's value. Recursively check both subtrees with updated ranges. If any node violates its range, return false.
tale: Imagine a kingdom where every noble has a strict rank, and their children must follow suit: left heirs must be of lower rank, right heirs of higher rank. A royal inspector visits each noble with a scroll listing the allowed rank range inherited from ancestors. At each stop, she checks if the noble's rank fits within the scroll's bounds. If not, the kingdom is in chaos. She updates the scroll and passes it down to the children. If she reaches the end of the family tree without finding a violator, the kingdom is orderly — a true BST.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Use DFS with min and max bounds. Start at the root with min = -infinity, max = +infinity. At each node, check if its value is within (min, max). If not, return false. Recurse left with updated max = node.val, and recurse right with updated min = node.val. If all nodes pass, return true.
solutions.tale: The inspector carries two scrolls: one for the lowest permitted rank (min), one for the highest (max). She arrives at the king with scrolls reading 'no limit' on both sides. She checks the king's rank against the scrolls — it fits. She hands the left scroll (with new upper limit = king's rank) to the left heir's inspector, and the right scroll (with new lower limit = king's rank) to the right heir's inspector. They repeat. If any inspector finds a mismatch, the alarm sounds. Otherwise, the dynasty is valid.
approach: Define a helper function that takes a node, a min, and a max.
If the node is null, return true (empty subtrees are valid BSTs).
Check if node.val is strictly between min and max. If not, return false.
Recursively validate the left subtree with updated max = node.val.
Recursively validate the right subtree with updated min = node.val.
Return true if both subtrees are valid.
solutions.pseudocode:
isValidBST(node, min, max):
  if node == null: return true
  if node.val <= min or node.val >= max: return false
  return isValidBST(node.left, min, node.val) AND
         isValidBST(node.right, node.val, max)

main:
  return isValidBST(root, -INF, +INF)

title: Sorted Array To Balanced BST
description:
Given an array where elements are sorted in ascending order, convert it to a height Balanced Binary Search Tree (BBST).

Balanced tree: a height-balanced binary tree is defined as a binary tree in which the depth of the two subtrees of every node never differ by more than 1.
story: Pick the middle as root. Left half becomes left subtree, right half becomes right subtree. Recursion balances automatically.
plain: To create a balanced BST from a sorted array, pick the middle element as the root (this ensures balance). Recursively build the left subtree from the left half of the array and the right subtree from the right half. The in-order traversal of the resulting tree will match the original sorted array, and the tree will be balanced because each split divides the array evenly.
tale: Imagine a librarian arranging books on shelves. She has a sorted list of titles and wants to build a retrieval tree so that finding any book takes roughly the same time. She picks the middle book as the root — this splits the collection into two equal halves. She repeats: middle of the left half becomes the left child, middle of the right half becomes the right child. By always splitting down the middle, the tree never leans to one side, keeping search times fast and balanced.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Use recursion with left and right pointers. Base case: if left > right, return null. Find the middle index. Create a node with the middle value. Recursively build the left subtree from [left, mid-1] and the right subtree from [mid+1, right]. Return the root.
solutions.tale: The librarian stands before a shelf holding all books. She picks the middle book and places it at the top of the tree. She hands the left half of books to her assistant, saying 'build a subtree from these,' and hands the right half to another assistant with the same instruction. Each assistant repeats the process: pick the middle, split, recurse. Eventually, every book finds its place, and the tree is perfectly balanced because every split was fair.
approach: Define a recursive helper function that takes the array, left index, and right index.
Base case: if left > right, return null.
Calculate mid = (left + right) / 2.
Create a new TreeNode with value nums[mid].
Recursively build left subtree from [left, mid-1].
Recursively build right subtree from [mid+1, right].
Return the root node.
solutions.pseudocode:
convert(nums, l, r):
  if l > r: return null
  mid = (l + r) / 2
  root = new TreeNode(nums[mid])
  root.left = convert(nums, l, mid - 1)
  root.right = convert(nums, mid + 1, r)
  return root

main:
  return convert(nums, 0, len(nums) - 1)

title: Delete a Node in BST
description:
Given a Binary Search Tree(BST) A. If there is a node with value B present in the tree delete it and return the tree.

Note - If there are multiple options, always replace a node by its in-order predecessor.
story: Find the node. If it has two children, replace it with its inorder predecessor (rightmost of left subtree), then delete that predecessor.
plain: To delete a node from a BST: first find it using BST search. If it's a leaf, just remove it. If it has one child, replace it with that child. If it has two children, find its inorder predecessor (the rightmost node in the left subtree), copy its value to the current node, then recursively delete the predecessor. This preserves BST order.
tale: A noble must be removed from the family tree. If they have no heirs, their branch simply ends. If they have one heir, that heir takes their place. If they have two heirs — left and right — the protocol is: find the highest-ranked person in the left branch (the rightmost), promote them to the vacant seat, then remove their old position. The tree reorganizes, and the BST order is preserved.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Recursively search for the target node. If not found, return unchanged. If found with 0 or 1 child, replace with that child. If found with 2 children, find the inorder predecessor (max in left subtree), copy its value to current node, then recursively delete the predecessor from the left subtree.
solutions.tale: The removal squad searches the tree for the target noble. When found, they assess: no children? Remove directly. One child? Promote the child. Two children? Send a scout down the left branch to find the rightmost noble (the immediate lower rank), copy that noble's credentials to the current seat, then remove the scout's original position. The tree heals itself.
approach: If root is null, return null.
If target < root.val, recurse left.
If target > root.val, recurse right.
If target == root.val, this is the node to delete:
- If no left child, return right child (covers leaf and 1-child cases).
- If no right child, return left child.
- If both children exist, find max in left subtree (inorder predecessor).
- Replace root.val with predecessor's val.
- Recursively delete predecessor from left subtree.
Return root.
solutions.pseudocode:
deleteNode(root, B):
  if root == null: return null
  if B < root.val: root.left = deleteNode(root.left, B)
  else if B > root.val: root.right = deleteNode(root.right, B)
  else:
    if root.left == null: return root.right
    if root.right == null: return root.left
    pred = findMax(root.left)
    root.val = pred.val
    root.left = deleteNode(root.left, pred.val)
  return root

title: Search in BST
description: Given a Binary Search Tree A. Check whether there exists a node with value B in the BST.
story: If target < root, go left. If target > root, go right. If equal, found. Else not found.
plain: BST search is binary search on a tree. Start at the root. If the target equals the current node's value, return true. If target is less, recurse left (all larger values are to the right, so we can ignore them). If target is greater, recurse right. If you reach null, the target doesn't exist.
tale: You are looking for a specific book in a library where shelves are organized left-to-right by ascending ID. You start at the middle shelf. If your book's ID matches, you're done. If your book's ID is smaller, you know it must be to the left, so you walk left and repeat. If larger, walk right. If you reach the end of a shelf (null), the book isn't in the library.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Start at root. If null, return 0 (not found). If root.val == B, return 1 (found). If B < root.val, recursively search left subtree. If B > root.val, recursively search right subtree. The BST property guarantees you only explore one path.
solutions.tale: The searcher stands at the root shelf and checks the label. Match? Done. Too low? She walks left, knowing the right half is all higher IDs. Too high? She walks right, discarding the left. She repeats until she either finds the book or runs out of shelves. No wasted steps — the tree guides her.
approach: If A is null, return 0.
If A.val == B, return 1.
If A.val > B, return searchInABST(A.left, B).
Else, return searchInABST(A.right, B).

title: Two Sum BST
description:
Given a binary search tree A, where each node contains a positive integer, and an integer B, you have to find whether or not there exist two different nodes X and Y such that X.value + Y.value = B.

Return 1 to denote that two such nodes exist. Return 0, otherwise.
story: Inorder traversal gives sorted array. Two-pointer or HashSet can find the pair.
plain: Convert the BST to a sorted array using inorder traversal (left-root-right). Then apply the two-sum algorithm: use two pointers (left and right) on the sorted array. If sum == target, return 1. If sum < target, move left pointer right. If sum > target, move right pointer left. Alternatively, use a HashSet: traverse the tree and for each node, check if (B - node.val) exists in the set.
tale: You are in a library where books are shelved by ID in ascending order (that's the BST). You need two books whose IDs sum to a specific total. First, you walk through the library from left to right, writing down all IDs in order — now you have a sorted list. Then you use two fingers: one at the start, one at the end. If their sum is too small, move the left finger right. If too large, move the right finger left. When the sum matches, you've found the pair.

solutions.label: Inorder + Two Pointers
solutions.plain: Do an inorder traversal to collect all values in a sorted list. Use two pointers: left starts at 0, right starts at end. While left < right, check sum. If sum == B, return 1. If sum < B, increment left. If sum > B, decrement right. If no pair found, return 0.
solutions.tale: The librarian walks the shelves left-to-right, writing down every book ID. Then she places one finger on the first ID, another on the last. She adds them. Too small? Move the left finger forward. Too large? Move the right finger backward. She repeats until she finds the exact sum or the fingers meet.
approach: Perform inorder traversal to get a sorted list of node values.
Initialize left = 0, right = list.size() - 1.
While left < right:
- Calculate sum = list[left] + list[right].
- If sum == B, return 1.
- If sum < B, increment left.
- If sum > B, decrement right.
Return 0 if no pair found.
solutions.pseudocode:
inorder(root, list):
  if root == null: return
  inorder(root.left, list)
  list.add(root.val)
  inorder(root.right, list)

twoSumBST(root, B):
  list = []
  inorder(root, list)
  left = 0, right = list.size() - 1
  while left < right:
    sum = list[left] + list[right]
    if sum == B: return 1
    if sum < B: left++
    else: right--
  return 0
solutions.story: Inorder gives sorted array, then two-pointer scan.

solutions.label: HashSet (One Pass)
solutions.plain: Traverse the tree (any order). For each node, check if (B - node.val) exists in a HashSet. If yes, return 1. Otherwise, add node.val to the set and continue. This avoids building the sorted array.
solutions.tale: An alternative librarian carries a notebook. As she visits each book, she checks if the notebook already has a complementary ID (the target minus current ID). If yes, she's found the pair. If not, she writes the current ID in the notebook and moves on. Faster, but less methodical than the two-finger approach.
approach: Initialize an empty HashSet.
Traverse the tree (DFS or BFS).
For each node, check if (B - node.val) is in the set.
If yes, return 1.
Otherwise, add node.val to the set.
If traversal ends, return 0.
solutions.pseudocode:
twoSumBSTHashSet(root, B, set):
  if root == null: return 0
  if set.contains(B - root.val): return 1
  set.add(root.val)
  return twoSumBSTHashSet(root.left, B, set) OR 
         twoSumBSTHashSet(root.right, B, set)

description: Given preorder traversal of a binary tree, check if it is possible that it is also a preorder traversal of a Binary Search Tree (BST), where each internal node (non-leaf nodes) have exactly one child.
story: Each internal node has exactly one child. Check if the sequence can form a valid BST with this constraint.
plain: In a BST where every internal node has exactly one child, the child is either always left (smaller) or always right (larger). For preorder, we process parent before child. So, for each element, all elements after it should be either all smaller (left-skewed) or all larger (right-skewed) until we hit a leaf or the end. Check if the sequence satisfies this: for each index, the remaining elements should form a monotonically increasing or decreasing subsequence consistent with BST property.
tale: Imagine a family tree where every parent has exactly one heir — either a younger sibling's child or an older one, but never both. A genealogist has a list of names in the order they were crowned (preorder). She checks: after each name, do all subsequent names follow a single direction — either all younger ranks or all older ranks? If the list zigzags (younger, then older, then younger again) without leaves in between, the tree is impossible. If the list is consistent, the tree is valid.

If you find both types (one smaller, one larger), return NO unless the transition happens at a leaf boundary. Alternatively, check for monotonic increasing or decreasing within each subtree segment. A simpler check: for a one-child BST, the preorder must form a sequence where each parent-child pair is either strictly increasing or strictly decreasing throughout.

If she finds a mix (some lower, some higher), she knows there must be two branches, which violates the one-child rule. If the list is clean — each segment moves in one direction — the tree is valid.

title: BST Nodes in a Range
description: Given a binary search tree of integers. You are given a range B and C. Return the count of the number of nodes that lie in the given range.
story: Use BST property to prune branches. If node < B, go right only. If node > C, go left only. Else count and explore both.
plain: To count nodes in range [B, C] in a BST, do a DFS. At each node, check if its value is in [B, C]. If yes, count it and explore both children. If node.val < B, all left children are also < B, so only explore right subtree. If node.val > C, all right children are also > C, so only explore left subtree. This prunes unnecessary branches using the BST property.
tale: A census taker is counting citizens in a certain age range [B, C]. The kingdom is organized as a BST by age. She starts at the capital (root). If the ruler's age is in range, she counts them and sends scouts to both provinces. If the ruler is too young (< B), she knows the left province (younger ages) is irrelevant, so she only checks the right. If the ruler is too old (> C), she skips the right and checks only the left. By pruning branches this way, she avoids visiting the entire kingdom.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Use DFS recursion. Base case: if node is null, return 0. Check node.val: if in [B, C], count = 1 + countRange(left) + countRange(right). If node.val < B, return countRange(right). If node.val > C, return countRange(left). This leverages BST to prune entire subtrees.
solutions.tale: The census taker stands at each node and makes three decisions: (1) am I in range? Count me. (2) Should I send a scout left? Only if my age >= B (otherwise left is too young). (3) Should I send a scout right? Only if my age <= C (otherwise right is too old). By making smart decisions, she avoids wasting scouts on regions that can't possibly hold in-range citizens.
approach: Define a recursive helper function countRange(node, B, C).
Base case: if node is null, return 0.
If node.val < B, return countRange(node.right, B, C) (left subtree is out of range).
If node.val > C, return countRange(node.left, B, C) (right subtree is out of range).
Otherwise, node.val is in [B, C], return 1 + countRange(node.left, B, C) + countRange(node.right, B, C).
